blocks.text: Erpenianus, referring it to the wings, rendered it thus: واجنحتهم مثل اتراس حديد [wa-ajniḥatuhum mithl atrās ḥadīd] And their wings were like iron shields. The other, however, referred it to the breast: وكانت صدورها مزردة كزرد حديد [wa-kānat ṣudūruhā muzarrada ka-zard ḥadīd] And their breasts were mailed as with breastplates of iron. What follows, that the sound of their wings was as the sound of chariots, of many horses running to battle, is taken from Ioelis II, 5. Like the sound of chariots they shall leap upon the tops of the mountains, etc. as a strong people set in battle array. Thus what has been noted so far John drew from the natural history of locusts. But now more features follow that are peculiar to these. Let the first of them be that the smoke by which they are cast down [III, 340] onto the earth does not come out of the chasm of the Acridophagi, but from the pit of the abyss, which is the chasm of the underworld. 2. That they harm neither the grass of the earth nor the trees of the field, but only those men who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads. 3. That they have in their tails the stings of scorpions, with which they torment men with a torment like the torment of a scorpion when it strikes a man. 4. To these are added crowns on their heads like gold. 5. And the faces of men. 6. And the hair of women. All these marks are lacking in real locusts. Finally, real locusts have no king, Prov. XXX, 27. But these have a king, and not one of their own kind, but the angel of the abyss, who in Hebrew is called אבדון Abaddon, and in Greek Ἀπολλύων [Apollyōn], not Ἀπόλλων [Apollōn], as the Syriac and the Ethiopic have it; both are taken from destroying. For אבד abad is the verb ἀπολλύειν [apollyein], and אבדון abaddon is ἀπώλεια [apōleia]. And if locusts had a king, this name would suit him, because [col. 496] destroying is the proper work of locusts. Hence Ioel I, 11, in Hebrew אבד קציר שרה, The harvest of the field has perished. And in Greek, Ἀπώλωλε τρύγητος ἐξ ἀγροῦ [Apōlōle trygētos ex agrou], The vintage has perished from the field, destroyed, that is, by locusts. But here, as other locusts are meant, so also another destruction, far different from that which common locusts bring. Its author is the angel of the abyss, that is, the devil, who, himself long since lost, is bent on this alone: to roll and thrust us too down into the same pit of perdition. Since he does this through the agency of the locusts that John describes, it would be worthwhile to show what those locusts are and to mark them out by their characteristics; but for certain reasons we refrain from this inquiry, being about to pass on to other matters.
